shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of France's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Zero point four percent. {p} That's how much the French economy grows this year, after inflation, in the IMF's estimate. Poland's: three point four. {pp} And that's how the gap closes. In 1990, the average Pole was at thirty-four percent of the average French person: income per person, adjusted for prices. Half by 2008. Seventy percent in 2019. Eighty-seven percent this year: about sixty thousand dollars against sixty-nine thousand. {p} The IMF has ninety percent in 2028, and ninety-five in 2031.

Last episode was Britain, and if these numbers sound familiar, there's a reason. This year, France and Britain are almost exactly as rich as each other per person: about sixty-eight thousand eight hundred dollars in France, sixty-eight thousand five hundred in Britain. {p} So Poland is catching both at the same speed. But France has its own story: the slowest growth of the two this year, the bigger debt, and the higher unemployment. {pp} <soft>Here's how fast the gap closed, where France still wins, and when Poland could pass it.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series, and the next episode is Spain, the country Poland passes next year in the IMF's forecast. Subscribe so you don't miss it. {p} Now, the long view.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Poland's GDP per capita, PPP, as % of France's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: In 1990, the average French person produced almost twenty thousand dollars a year, adjusted for prices. The average Pole, about six thousand seven hundred. In 2004, the year Poland joined the European Union: about thirty-two thousand five hundred in France, about fourteen and a half thousand in Poland. {p} Since then, Poland's economy has grown about three and a half times, after inflation. France's, about one point seven times. {pp} For the first eighteen years, Poland gained slowly: thirty-four percent in 1990, forty-five when it joined the European Union in 2004. Then, after 2008, the line gets steep: Poland gained almost thirty points on France in sixteen years, from fifty-two percent in 2008 to eighty-one in 2024.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, France (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's France's economy, year by year, after inflation. Since 1990, it has shrunk in only three years: 1993, 2009 and 2020. France's problem isn't crashes. It's slow growth. {p} The 2010s: about one and a half percent a year on average. Poland, in the same decade: almost four. {pp} 2020: minus seven and a half percent. Then a rebound, and then a slowdown: under one percent last year, zero point four this year. {p} And the IMF's forecast doesn't see much more: about one percent a year until 2031. Poland, in the same forecast: two and a half.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH), population (LP)
shots.title: Since 2019, and people
shots.narration: Put the last six years side by side: from 2019 to 2025, the French economy grew about six percent in total. Poland's grew about eighteen. {p} And there's population. Since 1990, France has grown from about fifty-eight million people to sixty-nine million. Poland has shrunk, from thirty-eight million to thirty-six. {pp} More people sharing slower growth means income per person rises slowly in France. Fewer people sharing faster growth means it rises fast in Poland. That's the whole race in one sentence.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ (NGDPDPC); inflation (PCPIPCH)
shots.title: Where France still wins
shots.narration: Now, what France still does better. First, plain dollars. Without adjusting for prices, the average French person produces about fifty-one thousand dollars this year, and the average Pole about thirty-one thousand. Poland is at sixty-one percent there, not eighty-seven. {p} In 1990, it was thirteen times more. Now it's less than twice. {pp} Second: inflation. In 2022, the year energy prices exploded, French inflation was about six percent, the lowest in the euro area, thanks partly to price caps on energy. Poland's was over fourteen. {p} So for a Polish worker, a salary in France still goes a lot further in plain euros, even if rent in Paris eats a big part of it.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. Spain is next. {p} Now, where Poland already wins.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · general government gross debt (% of GDP), 2026 estimate and 2031 forecast
shots.title: Government debt, % of GDP, 2026

cues.at: France's: about a hundred and nineteen

shots.narration: Government debt this year: Poland, about sixty-seven percent of its economy. {pp} France's: about a hundred and nineteen, and still rising in the IMF's forecast, to about a hundred and twenty-four by 2031. Poland's debt rises too in that forecast, to about eighty-two, but it starts much lower. {p} And unemployment: about three point two percent in Poland. In France, eight point four. More than two and a half times as high.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · PPPPC; parity years are Chartbound extrapolations of the 2016–2026 and IMF 2026–2031 paces, not IMF forecasts
shots.title: When does Poland pass France?
shots.narration: So, when does Poland pass France? {p} The gap in dollars, adjusted for prices, was widest in 2006: about eighteen thousand eight hundred. This year, it's about eight thousand eight hundred. In the IMF's forecast, about three thousand eight hundred by 2031. {p} Beyond that, two honest extrapolations. At the pace of the last ten years, when Poland gained almost three percent a year on France, it passes around 2031. At the IMF's slower pace, around 2034. {pp} The exact same dates we got for Britain. These two really are twins.

Think about what that means. In the early nineties, France was the kind of country Poles looked up to: three times richer per person, adjusted for prices. Within about a decade, by these numbers, the average Pole could produce as much as the average French person. {p} Prices, wages and pensions in plain euros will still be higher in France for a long time. But measured by what money actually buys, the race is nearly over.

<soft>So, your guess: 2031, 2034, or later?</soft> Tell me in the comments. {p} If you're watching from France: does zero point four percent feel right from where you are? {p} If you're in Poland: did you expect to be this close to France? {p} And Spain: you're next. I read every comment.
And if you missed it, Poland versus Britain is the twin of this one: eighty-eight percent, and the story of the Poles who moved there. That's right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

FRA vs GBR 2026: FRA slower growth (0.4 vs GBR), higher debt (118 vs 102), higher unemployment (8.4 vs 5.3) — GBR do A-L25
FRA avg 2010–2019 ≈ 1.4 (about one and a half), POL 3.8 (almost four)
FRA 2020 −7.6 (minus seven and a half); 2025 0.9 (under one percent); 2027–2031 0.7–1.2 (about one percent); POL 2027–2031 2.5
inflation 2022: FRA 5.9 (about six; HICP mais baixo da zona do euro — Eurostat), POL 14.4 (over fourteen)
debt: POL 2026 ≈ 67; FRA 2026 118.5 (tela mostra 119 → narração 'a hundred and nineteen'), 2031 ≈ 124, rising

yt.title: France Grew 0.4% This Year. Poland Is Closing In.
yt.description:
Income per person, adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): Poland was 34% of France in 1990, half in 2008, 70% in 2019 and 87% this year; the IMF has 90% in 2028 and 95% in 2031. France grows 0.4% this year in the IMF's estimate, Poland 3.4%. France and Britain are now almost exactly as rich per person, so Poland is catching both at the same speed. Plain dollars (Poland 61%), inflation, debt (118% vs 67%), unemployment (8.4% vs 3.2%), and two dates for parity: ~2031 at the 2016–2026 pace, ~2034 at the IMF's pace.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP, LUR, GGXWDG_NGDP, PCPIPCH). Parity years are extrapolations, not IMF forecasts.
